00 · Week overview

W2: Text Preparation in R and Python: Collaborative Workflow

W1 argued that "text can be treated as data"; in W2 we actually turn text into data: selecting documents, cleaning, tokenizing, and building a DFM (document-feature matrix), asking at every step: "What does this choice make my measurement lose?"

In this chapter
Learning objectivesConcept mapThe two practice datasetsHow to use these notesSelf-check

Learning objectives for this week Slide 2

Slide 2 lists four objectives; the last one (clean and tokenize text, build a DFM, and evaluate preprocessing choices) is the backbone of these notes. The instructor also points out that this is Week 4 content introduced early; W4 builds on it with dictionaries, sentiment analysis, and validation.

  1. Set up RStudio and Positron for text analysis with R and Python.
  2. Organize code with GitHub and submit written coursework through shared Overleaf projects.
  3. Inspect supplied corpora and check project data feasibility: coverage, metadata, and access.
  4. Clean and tokenize text, build a DFM, and evaluate preprocessing choices.

Lab: a sample of UK House of Commons speeches Slide 61
  • lab/Data/hc_sample_1945_2025.rds: 5,000 House of Commons speech contributions, 1945–2025.
  • 13 columns: date, agenda, speechnumber, speaker, party, party.facts.id, chair, terms, text, speech_url, parliament, iso3country, party_raw.

  • 5,000 is the number of speeches, not the number of MPs: the same MP can speak many times.

01 · Principles and selecting documents

Five QTA principles and selecting documents

Bias begins before preprocessing. This chapter covers where texts come from, whose texts are more likely to be preserved, and what a "document" is.

In this chapter
Five principlesSelecting documents (coffee example)Selection biasInteractive: spot the biasCorpus boundaries and document unitsImport routesSelf-check

Five principles of quantitative text analysis Slide 3

  1. Domain knowledge defines the research problem and relevant evidence.
  2. Human judgment guides interpretation and validation.
  3. Discovery and testing require distinct stages.
  4. The task determines which methods are useful.
  5. Validation evaluates whether the measure fits the claim.

Sources: Schoonvelde (2026); Grimmer et al. (2022).Slide 3

In plain words · Supplement (not from the lecture)

Computers only count; what to count, how to interpret it, and whether the counts can support your conclusion are the researcher's responsibility. These five principles come back at every preprocessing choice.

Selecting documents: Chapter 4 of Grimmer et al. (2022) Slide 4

Classroom example: measuring expressed preference for coffee.

Design choiceExample
Target populationThai-language public posts about coffee in a specified month
Quantity of interestShare of those posts expressing positive preference for coffee
Observed corpusPosts returned by one platform API and a specified keyword search

Found data: document how the texts were produced, preserved and retrieved. The next step is to examine what the collection process leaves out.Slide 4

02 · Tool landscape

The tool landscape: quanteda, UDPipe, spaCy, Flair, and R + Python

R can prepare text, call these tools, and analyze the returned annotations or vectors. The tools overlap, and their capabilities depend on the language, model, and task.

In this chapter
The R toolkit in 2017Beyond 2017: annotation and embeddingsComparing four toolsFlip cardsUsing R and Python togetherPositronSelf-check

The R text-analysis toolkit in 2017 Slide 8

Slide 8 reproduces Table 1 of Welbers, Van Atteveldt & Benoit (2017) (text-analysis operations and the corresponding R packages) and notes that this is a historical package overview (2017); package responsibilities and APIs have since changed. The original Table 1 groups the operations into three parts: data preparation (importing text, string operations, preprocessing, DTM, filtering and weighting), analysis (dictionary, supervised / unsupervised machine learning, text statistics), and advanced topics (advanced NLP, word positions and syntax). (Welbers et al. 2017, p. 247)

R and Python in one workflow Slides 11–12

One possible application on slide 11: compare the meanings of policy statements.

→ →

Static version: Prepare in R (stringr, quanteda: clean text and preserve document IDs) → Represent in Python (sentence-transformers: encode texts as semantic vectors) → Evaluate in R (statistical models and plots: validate similarities and interpret patterns). Each stage follows the research question.Slide 11

Python inside an R session Slide 12
  • R's reticulate package imports Python modules and calls their functions.
  • The instructor frequently used reticulate during their PhD studies (2018–2022).
  • It converts supported objects between R and Python.
  • Record the Python environment as well as R packages.
Separate scripts, shared data Slide 12
  • R and Python scripts exchange files such as CSV or Parquet.
  • A stable document ID connects inputs and outputs.
  • Check row order, encoding and data types at each handoff.

The takeaway of slide 12: an IDE organizes the work; object or file exchange connects the languages.

Positron: one IDE for R and Python Slide 13

  • In 2022, RStudio the company became Posit, reflecting its broader support for data science across languages.
  • Posit developed Positron for multilingual data science; R and Python have built-in support, with consoles and data exploration.
  • The RStudio IDE remains a separate, maintained product.
  • Our classroom examples use R.

03 · Workflow and objects

Text-analysis steps, four objects, and import checks

Analysis can take the "matrix" route (DFM), or it can keep token positions or other representations. First be clear about which kind of object you are holding.

In this chapter
Order of operationsFour objectsImport checks and encodingA parliamentary exampleInteractive: sorting exerciseSelf-check

The sequence of text-analysis operations Slide 14

Slide 14 reproduces Figure 1 of Welbers et al. (2017) (Order of text analysis operations for data preparation and analysis, p. 247). The slide's reminder: the branch matters—analysis can use a matrix, token positions, or other representations. Welbers et al. focus mainly on bag-of-words, i.e., using only the word frequencies of each text and ignoring word positions (p. 246), and discuss approaches that keep word positions and syntax under advanced topics (pp. 258–261).

Objects used in this session Slide 15

ObjectContentsUse
Data frameText, identifiers, metadataImport checks and joins
corpusText with document variables (docvars)Subsets and metadata access
tokensSequences of tokens (order preserved)Phrase matching and context inspection (KWIC)
dfmDocuments × featuresCounts and weighted representations

stringr handles strings. quanteda provides the corpus → tokens → DFM workflow.Slide 15

→ → →
  • data.frame: the Lab's hoc, one row per speech; text and metadata are all columns.
  • corpus: corpus(hoc, text_field = "text"); the other columns become docvars, still 5,000 documents.
  • tokens: each document becomes a sequence of words; you can use tokens_compound() and kwic().
  • dfm: only counts remain and order is gone; you can use dfm_group(), dfm_trim(), textstat_keyness().

Import checks and encoding Slide 16

R · slide 16 (sketch; the file path is the slide's example)
texts <- readLines("data/speeches.txt", encoding = "UTF-8")
length(texts)
head(texts)
  • Confirm the source encoding rather than guessing from appearance.
  • Inspect accented characters and Chinese text after import.
  • Count missing texts and duplicated identifiers.
  • Check whether a row is a line, paragraph, or whole document.
The key warning on slide 16

Adding an encoding = "UTF-8" argument does not repair text whose source encoding was wrongly identified.Slide 16

A real example from the Lab data (local R output)

The Lab's collocation output contains sinn fã (count 15), and the same table also has sinn fein (count 17). The é in "Féin" was most likely decoded with the wrong encoding somewhere upstream in the data processing and turned into garbled text (mojibake), so the same party name was split into two features. This is exactly why slide 16 asks you to "inspect accented characters" after import. (Output in Chapter 11, find_collocations; the diagnosis of the cause is an inference made in these notes, not from the lecture.)

04 · Cleaning and regex

Cleaning depends on the research question: stringr and regular expressions

Cleaning is not neutral. Every rule keeps some information and throws some away; that is why you need an audit trail.

In this chapter
stringr functionsBrackets and unintended deletionInteractive: greedy vs. non-greedyCleaning with an audit trailInteractive: regex playground (real data)Self-check

String operations with stringr Slide 19

FunctionPurposeExample use
str_detect()Test whether a pattern appears (TRUE / FALSE)Flag bracketed annotations
str_extract()Retrieve the first matchExtract a year
str_remove_all()Remove all matchesDelete selected annotations
str_replace_all()Replace matchesStandardize separators
str_squish()Normalize whitespaceRemove repeated spaces and leading/trailing whitespace
str_to_lower()Change caseMerge case variants

The Lab also uses str_which() (which positions match), str_locate() / str_locate_all() (start and end character positions of matches), str_extract_all(), and str_to_title(); see Chapter 10.

Bracket patterns and unintended deletion Slide 20

R · S02 Bracket patterns (slide 20) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
s <- "Trade [Commons] and jobs [Wales]"
str_remove_all(s, "\\[.*\\]")
str_remove_all(s, "\\[[^\\[\\]]*\\]") |> str_squish()
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> s <- "Trade [Commons] and jobs [Wales]"
> str_remove_all(s, "\\[.*\\]")
[1] "Trade "
> str_remove_all(s, "\\[[^\\[\\]]*\\]") |> str_squish()
[1] "Trade and jobs"
"\\[.*\\]"
.* is greedy: it consumes everything from the first [ to the last ], deleting the “and jobs” in between as well and leaving only "Trade ".
"\\[[^\\[\\]]*\\]"
[^\\[\\]]* means "any number of characters that are not brackets", so each bracket group is removed separately; then str_squish() tidies up the extra whitespace → "Trade and jobs".

The slide: the second pattern handles separate, non-nested bracket groups.Slide 20

Interactive: greedy vs. non-greedy bracket removal

🧪Bracket-removal comparatorToy intuition · Supplement (not from the lecture); default string from slide 20
RuleResult
str_remove_all(s, "\\[.*\\]")
str_remove_all(s, "\\[[^\\[\\]]*\\]") |> str_squish()
The Lab's rule str_replace_all(s, "\\s*\\[.*\\]", "")

A cleaning example with an audit trail Slide 21

R · S03 Cleaning with an audit trail (slide 21; week2.qmd clean-agenda) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
agenda_raw <- "  Export Trade [Commons] -- vol. 407  "
agenda_clean <- agenda_raw |>
  str_remove_all("\\[[^\\[\\]]*\\]") |>
  str_to_lower() |>
  str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]]", " ") |>
  str_squish()
agenda_clean
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> agenda_raw <- "  Export Trade [Commons] -- vol. 407  "
> agenda_clean <- agenda_raw |>
+   str_remove_all("\\[[^\\[\\]]*\\]") |>
+   str_to_lower() |>
+   str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]]", " ") |>
+   str_squish()
> agenda_clean
[1] "export trade vol 407"
str_remove_all("\\[[^\\[\\]]*\\]")
Deletes [Commons].
str_to_lower()
Lowercases everything: Export Trade → export trade.
str_replace_all("[^[:alnum:][:space:]]", " ")
Replaces characters that are "neither alphanumeric nor whitespace" (--, .) with a space.
str_squish()
Collapses runs of whitespace into one and trims leading and trailing whitespace.

This rule preserves numbers and removes punctuation; another task may need a different rule.Slide 21 An "audit trail" means storing the cleaned result in a new column (the Lab uses agenda_clean) while keeping the original column, so you can compare them at any time.

Interactive: regex playground (real Lab agenda labels)

🔤Regex playgroundReal data · 5,000 agenda values

The data are the Lab's hoc$agenda (4,000+ distinct labels with their counts, exported from R; plus 206 NA). Enter a pattern to see how many speeches match, with the top 12 labels listed (matches highlighted). JS regex is broadly similar to R/stringr (ICU) but not identical (for example, the POSIX class [:alnum:] is not supported in JS); R gives the authoritative result. Type a single backslash here (JS style); in an R string you need two.

Matching speeches
–
Distinct matching labels

Check

Try it: compare war and \bwar\b. Which labels are the extra ones?

war also matches words that contain these three letters, such as “warfare”, “towards”, “award”, and “Stewart”; \bwar\b matches only the standalone word, but “post-war” still counts because the hyphen is treated as a word boundary. The Lab's word_boundary_examples demonstrates exactly this (Chapter 10). Whether post-war should count depends on the research question.

05 · Toy corpus

A four-sentence toy corpus: corpus, tokens, and types

Using four sentences short enough to check word by word, we look closely at what R does at each step. All R output in this chapter comes from actually running the slides' source code (the setup chunk of week2.qmd) locally.

In this chapter
Creating a corpusTokens and typesInteractive: token / type counterR tokens vs. LLM tokensTokenizing with explicit choicesSelf-check

Creating a corpus Slides 22–23

R · S01 Slide worked example: four synthetic texts (week2.qmd setup; slides 22-23) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
library(quanteda)
library(stringr)
raw <- data.frame(
  doc_id = c("d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"),
  text = c("Health workers need health services.",
           "The government supports health services.",
           "Workers do not support the policy.",
           "The government supports the policy."),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
corp <- corpus(raw, docid_field = "doc_id", text_field = "text")
docnames(corp)
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> library(quanteda)
Package version: 4.5.1
Unicode version: 17.0
ICU version: 78.3
Parallel computing: 2 of 2 threads used.
See https://quanteda.io for tutorials and examples.
> library(stringr)
> raw <- data.frame(
+   doc_id = c("d1", "d2", "d3", "d4"),
+   text = c("Health workers need health services.",
+            "The government supports health services.",
+            "Workers do not support the policy.",
+            "The government supports the policy."),
+   stringsAsFactors = FALSE
+ )
> corp <- corpus(raw, docid_field = "doc_id", text_field = "text")
> docnames(corp)
[1] "d1" "d2" "d3" "d4"

Each row supplies one text. The remaining columns become document variables (docvars). Here docid_field = "doc_id" makes the document names d1–d4 instead of the default text1–text4.Slide 23

Compare with the Lab

The Lab's corpus(hoc, text_field = "text") does not specify docid_field, so the document names are text1…text5000 (see the summary output in Chapter 10). If you later hand data to Python or other files, slide 12 recommends a stable document ID.

Tokens, types, and vocabulary Slide 24

Text: “Health services need health workers.”

RepresentationTokensDistinct types
Case and punctuation retained66
Lowercase, punctuation removed54

After normalization: health, services, need, health, workers. A token is an occurrence. A type is a distinct form under the chosen representation.Slide 24

R · S04 Tokens and types (slide 24) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
t24 <- "Health services need health workers."
t_keep <- tokens(t24)
t_norm <- tokens(t24, remove_punct = TRUE) |> tokens_tolower()
c(tokens = ntoken(t_keep), types = ntype(t_keep))
c(tokens = ntoken(t_norm), types = ntype(t_norm))
as.character(t_norm)
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> t24 <- "Health services need health workers."
> t_keep <- tokens(t24)
> t_norm <- tokens(t24, remove_punct = TRUE) |> tokens_tolower()
> c(tokens = ntoken(t_keep), types = ntype(t_keep))
tokens.text1  types.text1 
           6            6 
> c(tokens = ntoken(t_norm), types = ntype(t_norm))
tokens.text1  types.text1 
           5            4 
> as.character(t_norm)
[1] "health"   "services" "need"     "health"   "workers"

Verified locally in R: ntoken() / ntype() give 6 / 6 and 5 / 4, matching slide 24. With case retained, “Health” and “health” are two types, and the period is also a token.

Tokens in R text analysis and LLMs Slide 25

ComparisonCommon R text-analysis workflowTypical LLM workflow
Common unitsWords; optionally characters or sentencesOften subwords; can include whole words, characters or byte units
Segmentation depends onPackage, tokenizer and your settingsThe model’s tokenizer and vocabulary
Main useWord counts, DFM, TF-IDF, topic modelsToken IDs used for model input and text generation

One word can become several LLM tokens. R can call either kind of tokenizer; the workflow determines the unit.Slide 25

Tokenizing with explicit choices Slide 26

R · S05 Tokenizing with explicit choices (slide 26) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
toks <- tokens(corp, remove_punct = TRUE) |>

06 · Preprocessing choices

Preprocessing choices and information loss

The key question on slide 27: how does the choice affect the intended measure? Not "what is the standard practice?"

In this chapter
Gains and losses of four choicesStopwords and negationBag-of-wordsWhat counts cannot recoverMultiword expressionsBigrams and order of operationsCollocations and grammatical featuresStemming vs. lemmatizationInteractive: preprocessing switchboardSelf-check

Preprocessing choices and information loss Slide 27

ChoicePossible benefitPossible loss
LowercaseMerge Health and healthProper-name distinctions
Remove stopwordsReduce frequent function wordsNegation or writing style
Stem or lemmatizeMerge some word formsDifferences in meaning
Trim rare featuresReduce vocabulary sizeRare but important concepts

Stopwords and negation Slide 28

R · S06 Stopwords and negation, document d3 (slide 28) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
sw <- setdiff(stopwords("en"), c("not", "no", "nor"))
toks_content <- tokens_remove(toks, pattern = sw)
as.character(tokens_remove(toks, pattern = stopwords("en"))["d3"])
as.character(toks_content["d3"])
length(stopwords("en"))

[1] "workers" "not"     "support" "policy"

Rule applied to document d3Remaining tokens
Standard English stopword listworkers support policy
List that retains negationworkers not support policy

Retaining not preserves a clue; but a unigram model still needs a way to use its scope.Slide 28 The local output confirms that stopwords("en") has 175 words and that not, no, and nor are all in it.

The bag-of-words representation Slide 29

A DFM stores one row per document and one column per feature. Below are selected columns from the count DFM built from the "negation-retaining" tokens:

R · S07 Selected DFM columns (slide 29) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)

as.matrix(x[, c("health", "workers", "government", "policy", "not")])

Identical to the table on slide 29 (health = 2 for d1). Features can also represent phrases or other categories.

What word counts cannot recover Slide 30

After lowercasing, “Workers support government.” and “Government support workers.” have exactly the same unigram counts:

R · S08 Word order is lost (slide 30) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
wo <- tokens(c(a = "Workers support government.", b = "Government support workers."),
             remove_punct = TRUE) |> tokens_tolower() |> dfm()
as.matrix(wo)
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> wo <- tokens(c(a = "Workers support government.", b = "Government support workers."),
+              remove_punct = TRUE) |> tokens_tolower() |> dfm()
> as.matrix(wo)
    features
docs workers support government
   a       1       1          1
   b       1       1          1
  • Word order tells you who supports whom.
  • Negation requires relations between words.
  • Ambiguous words need context.
  • Irony may depend on context beyond the sentence.

N-grams and syntax can preserve some additional information.Slide 30 (The R check that the two rows above have identical counts was run additionally for these notes.)

Multiword expressions Slide 31

R · S09 Multiword expressions (slide 31) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
phrase_toks <- tokens(
  "We support the armed forces.",
  remove_punct = TRUE
) |> tokens_tolower()
tokens_compound(
  phrase_toks,
  pattern = phrase("armed forces")
)
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> phrase_toks <- tokens(
+   "We support the armed forces.",
+   remove_punct = TRUE
+ ) |> tokens_tolower()
> tokens_compound(

+   pattern = phrase("armed forces")

tokens of 1 document (4 tokens, 4 types).
text1 :
[1] "we"           "support"      "the"          "armed_forces"

armed_forces becomes a single feature. Detect phrases before deleting words that may be part of them.Slide 31 The Lab uses the same method to merge “Prime Minister”, “House of Commons”, “European Union”, and “National Health Service” (Chapter 11).

Bigrams and the order of operations Slide 32

R · S10 Bigrams and operation order (slide 32) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
tokens("Workers do not support the policy.",
       remove_punct = TRUE) |>
  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_ngrams(n = 2)
tokens("Workers do not support the policy.",

  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) |>
  tokens_ngrams(n = 2)
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> tokens("Workers do not support the policy.",
+        remove_punct = TRUE) |>
+   tokens_tolower() |>
+   tokens_ngrams(n = 2)
tokens of 1 document (5 tokens, 5 types).
text1 :
[1] "workers_do"  "do_not"      "not_support" "support_the" "the_policy" 

> tokens("Workers do not support the policy.",
+        remove_punct = TRUE) |>
+   tokens_tolower() |>
+   tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) |>
+   tokens_ngrams(n = 2)
tokens of 1 document (2 tokens, 2 types).
text1 :
[1] "workers_support" "support_policy"

The bigrams on the slide: workers_do, do_not, not_support, support_the, the_policy. If the original adjacency matters, create bigrams before removing stopwords. Deleting words first creates pairs that were not originally adjacent.Slide 32 The second output above (run additionally for these notes) shows the consequence of doing it the other way round: after the standard stopword list deletes do, not, and the, a workers_support that does not exist in the original text is produced, and the negation disappears entirely.

Collocations and grammatical features Slide 33

Feature strategyExampleJudgment needed
Known phrasearmed_forcesWhich phrases matter?
Statistical collocationCandidates such as northern_irelandIs the association substantively useful?
Selection by part of speech (POS)Nouns, verbs, adjectivesWhich grammatical roles fit the task?

Frequent or strongly associated word pairs are only candidate features; inspect their usage before adding them to a measurement rule.Slide 33 In the Lab's real output, northern ireland occurs 338 times with λ ≈ 12.41 (Chapter 11).

Stemming and lemmatization Slide 34

MethodExampleLimitation
Stemmingstudies → studiA stem may not be a dictionary word
Lemmatizationstudies may → studyAccuracy depends on language and context
Explicit replacementMap forces to forceOnly handles the mappings you provide

Neither method guarantees correct semantic grouping. A dictionary built from full words may fail to match stemmed features.Slide 34 Welbers et al. (2017, p. 252) also point out an ordering issue: if you stem before removing stopwords, “during” becomes “dure” and no longer matches “during” in the stopword list.

07 · Multilingual text and UDPipe

Multilingual text: English whitespace is not a universal word boundary

Chinese, Japanese, and Thai need segmentation models; stopwords and word-form tools are tied to a language. UDPipe gives you tokens, parts of speech (POS), and dependency relations.

In this chapter
Language and model requirementsUDPipe modelsAnnotation codeInteractive: segmentation and dependency viewerModel errors and negationFrom syntax to a research measureAnnotations as DFM featuresSelf-check
Data sources for this chapter (stated plainly)

The UDPipe output on slides 38–42 consists of model predictions that the instructor transcribed from an earlier presentation HTML into the slide source (week2.qmd); slide 36 also notes that it is a "speaker demonstration: interpreting prepared model output". These notes did not rerun UDPipe (that requires downloading language models, and Thai also requires calling the UDPipe 2 REST API); the interactive components below use these slide outputs, each labeled with its slide number.

Language and model requirements Slide 35

Language
  • English whitespace is not a universal word boundary.
  • Chinese segmentation needs inspection.
  • Stopwords and word-form tools are language-specific.
Model
  • A DFM can use word or phrase features.
  • Pretrained models expect their own tokenizer.
  • Preserve the input distinctions that the model needs.

A BoW preprocessing recipe should not automatically become an LLM input recipe.Slide 35

UDPipe models: Japanese, Chinese, Thai Slide 36

Input languageAccess from RModel
Japaneseudpipe: local UDPipe 1japanese-gsd (UD 2.5)
Traditional Chineseudpipe: local UDPipe 1chinese-gsd (UD 2.5)
Thaihttr2: UDPipe 2 APIthai-tud (UD 2.17)
  • All three provide segmented tokens and predicted upos (POS).
  • Dependency parsing adds heads and relation labels.
  • lemma is the predicted base form; this Thai model returns _ (not available).

Annotating UTF-8 text with UDPipe Slide 37

R · slide 37 (not run for these notes: requires downloading the chinese-gsd model first)
library(udpipe)
# Set model_path to a downloaded Chinese-GSD model.
zh_model <- udpipe_load_model(model_path)
ann_zh <- udpipe_annotate(zh_model, x = "我喜歡咖啡。",
  doc_id = "zh_coffee", parser = "default") |> as.data.frame()
ann_zh[c("token_id", "token", "upos",
  "head_token_id", "dep_rel")]
  • parser = "default" adds dependency syntax on top of tokens and POS.
  • head_token_id identifies the head; dep_rel labels the relation. Head 0 marks the sentence root.
  • Chinese uses chinese-gsd; English uses english-ewt; Thai uses R + the UDPipe 2 API.Slide 37

Interactive: segmentation and dependency viewer (output from slides 38–42)

🌳Segmentation and dependency viewerInteractive summary · Supplement (not from the lecture); data = UDPipe output on slides 38–42

The segmentation comparison on slide 38 (excluding punctuation): Thai has 3 tokens (ฉัน PRON / ชอบ VERB / กาแฟ NOUN), so the Thai model finds word boundaries; Japanese has 6 tokens (私 PRON / は ADP / コーヒー NOUN / が ADP / 好き ADJ / です AUX), so particles and auxiliaries remain separate tokens; Chinese has 3 tokens (我 PRON / 喜歡 VERB / 咖啡 NOUN), so multi-character words can form single tokens. Slide 39: "I like coffee" in all three languages is nsubj / root / obj, with head IDs 2 / 0 / 2 in each case.Slides 38–39

Model errors and negation Slides 40–42

  • Japanese “政府は医療従事者を支援する。”: 政府 (NOUN, nsubj → 6), 医療 (compound → 4), 従事者 (obj → 6), 支援 (VERB, root), する (AUX).Slide 40
  • Traditional Chinese “政府支持醫療工作者。”: a model error—支持 is tagged NOUN, and 者 (PART) is predicted as root. The slide's reminder: inspect the original sentence before interpreting these outputs.Slide 41
  • Negation “政府不支持刪減醫療預算。”: 不 (ADV) attaches to 支持 (ID 3) as advmod. Keeping only NOUN and VERB removes “不”, so the feature list loses the negation.Slide 42 (Pick this sentence in the viewer above and try unticking ADV.)

From Thai syntax to research measurement Slide 43

→ → →

Static version: POS marks word classes, and dependency relations link the subject to the predicate and its object → link the subject to “like” and its object, and confirm the statement is affirmative → this example: positive preference for coffee = 1 → research question: which objects receive more expressions of positive preference? Corpus-level measurement: the share of documents mentioning an object that express positive preference. Arrows point from head to dependent.Slide 43 This also echoes the “coffee preference” research design from Chapter 01, slide 4.

Turning UDPipe annotations into quanteda tokens and a DFM Slides 44–45

R · Slide 44 (code sketch; ann_multi is an annotation table)
# Assume ann_multi contains an annotation table.
a <- subset(ann_multi, upos != "PUNCT")
a <- a[order(a$doc_id, a$sentence_id,
             as.integer(a$token_id)), ]
ja_tokens <- split(a$token[a$doc_id == "ja_01"],
                   a$doc_id[a$doc_id == "ja_01"])
ja_dfm <- dfm(as.tokens(ja_tokens), tolower = FALSE)

Use as.tokens() to keep the existing segmentation; a Chinese DFM is built the same way.Slide 44

🧮Same tokens, three kinds of DFM columnsToy intuition · Supplement (not from the lecture); content based on slide 45

A: workers (NOUN) / support (VERB) / reform (NOUN); B: workers (NOUN) / oppose (VERB) / reform (NOUN). The POS tags are the illustrative tags shown on the slide.

Rows = documents; columns = the features you chose; cells = counts. Noun filtering loses the stance contrast; dictionary counts still need validation.Slide 45

Note supports vs. support

Among the 9 features, supports (d2, d4) and support (d3) are two different features. Merging them requires stemming, lemmatization or an explicit replacement (Chapter 06, slide 34)—and each method has a cost.

Term frequency and document frequency Slide 47

R · S12 Term and document frequency; trimming (slide 47) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)

The threshold min_docfreq = 2 removes not. Rare features can still carry crucial meaning.Slide 47 The local output (featnames(x_trim) above) shows 6 features left after trimming: health, workers, services, government, supports, policy; need, not and support with df = 1 are dropped—even support (the only verb in d3) disappears.

Counts, binary indicators and TF-IDF Slide 48

RepresentationWhat a cell meansPossible use
CountNumber of occurrencesFrequency-based measurement
BinaryWhether the feature appearsComparison by presence/absence
TF-IDFCount adjusted by how common the feature is in the corpusDocument retrieval or comparison

The choice changes how much repeated words contribute. Model requirements may restrict which representation is appropriate.Slide 48

Writing out the TF-IDF formula Slides 49–50

This course uses raw counts and base-10 logarithms:

TF-IDF(d, t) = count(d, t) × log10(N / df(t))

  • N is the number of documents in the reference corpus; df(t) is the number of documents containing feature t.
  • A feature that appears in every document has IDF = 0 under this formula.
  • Different normalization and smoothing rules produce different weights.Slide 49
R · S13 TF-IDF in the worked example (slides 49-50) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
x_weighted <- dfm_tfidf(x, scheme_tf = "count",
                        scheme_df = "inverse", base = 10)
round(as.matrix(x_weighted[, "health"]), 4)
round(as.matrix(x_weighted), 4)
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> x_weighted <- dfm_tfidf(x, scheme_tf = "count",
+                         scheme_df = "inverse", base = 10)
> round(as.matrix(x_weighted[, "health"]), 4)
    features
docs health
  d1 0.6021
  d2 0.3010
  d3 0.0000
  d4 0.0000
> round(as.matrix(x_weighted), 4)

  d4 0.0000   0.000 0.0000    0.000      0.301    0.301 0.0000  0.0000  0.301

health: N = 4, df = 2, so IDF = log10(2) ≈ 0.3010; d1 count 2 → 0.6021, d2 count 1 → 0.3010, d3 and d4 are 0. Local R matches slide 50 exactly.Slide 50

Checking context with KWIC Slide 51

R · S14 KWIC (slide 51) (W2 slides week2.qmd, reconstructed from the slides for these notes)
kwic(toks, pattern = "support*", window = 3)
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)

Three matches: d2 “the government supports health services”, d3 “workers do not support the policy”, d4 “the government supports the policy”. Before treating a word count as evidence of “support for a policy”, read the words around it—in d3, support is directly preceded by not.Slide 51

Note: KWIC uses toks (tokens before stopword removal), so not and the are visible. The pattern "support*" is a glob wildcard that matches support and supports.

09 · Research uses and sensitivity

What is a DFM used for? And: how sensitive are results to preprocessing?

The same DFM can feed many methods, but each method has different input requirements: Wordfish and topic models need counts, classification needs training labels, Wordscores needs reference scores, and similarity can use TF-IDF.

In this chapter
DFM, KWIC, TF-IDF wrap-upResearch applications overviewInteractive: method matchingApplied studiesSensitivity checksSelf-check

Wrap-up: DFM, KWIC, TF-IDF Slide 52

ToolWhat it lets you do
DFMRepresent document features for comparison and modelling
KWICRead words in context to check what feature counts mean
TF-IDFEmphasize distinctive words for retrieval and similarity

Wordfish is an unsupervised method that places texts on one dimension: word-count DFM → Wordfish → relative positions of documents. Use: comparing party manifestos or speeches. Input: counts, not TF-IDF weights. Interpret and validate the scale before calling it “ideology”.Slide 52

Research applications of a DFM Slide 53

Research goalMethodOutput
Estimate positionsWordfish / WordscoresRelative positions of documents
Predict categoriesSupervised classifierIssue or stance labels
Study issue attentionLDA / STM / keyATMTopics and topic proportions
Measure a conceptDictionaryCategory counts or proportions
Compare documentsCosine similarity / clusteringSimilarity or document clusters

Inputs matter: Wordfish and these topic models use counts; classification needs training labels; Wordscores needs reference scores; similarity can use TF-IDF.Slide 53 These methods are covered in depth in W4 (dictionaries), W7 (scaling), W8 (topic models) and other weeks.

Interactive: method matching

🧭Research goal → method → required inputPractice · based on slides 52–53

Pick one method for each item; after answering, the input that method needs (counts, labels, reference scores or TF-IDF) is shown. The scenarios were written for these notes (supplement).

Applied studies introduced in the slides Slides 54–58

CategoryStudyOne-line summary on the slides
Topic modelsSTM: Roberts et al. (2014)Compare topics in survey responses across respondent groups.Slide 54
Topic modelskeyATM: Eshima et al. (2024)Guide topics with selected keywords to study policy attention.Slide 54
Text scalingWordfish: Slapin & Proksch (2008)Estimate relative party positions from word counts in manifestos. Corpus: 25 German party manifestos from five parties over five elections (1990–2005); finding: the Greens moved toward the centre over time; reading the axis: higher values mean left, and the sign is a convention (Figure 1A, p. 714).Slides 55–56
Text scalingWordscores: Lowe (2008); Laver et al. (2003)Position new texts using reference texts with known scores. Irish confidence debate: 3 reference speeches (+1 / −1) → score the other 55 speeches; higher scores mean more pro-government (Laver et al. 2003, Figure 3, p. 328).Slides 55, 57
TF-IDFText similarity: Blumenau (2021)Track whose language later speakers use in House of Commons debates.Slide 58
TF-IDFStance classification: Bestvater & Monroe (2023)Classify political support or opposition with TF-IDF plus SVM.Slide 58

TF-IDF provides weighted features; the analysis determines what we measure.Slide 58 The full texts of these papers are not in the course repo; these notes only restate what is on the slides (see Chapter 13).

Sensitivity to preprocessing Slide 59

ComparisonCheckInterpretation
With / without stopwordsNegation and grammatical contextWhich distinctions disappear?
Unigrams / phrasesCompound conceptsWhich matches change?
Full / trimmed vocabularyDropped features and empty rowsWhich documents lose evidence?
Counts / TF-IDFRelative contribution of featuresDo results depend on weighting?

Keep the corpus and research question fixed while comparing a chosen rule.Slide 59 The “preprocessing switch lab” in Chapter 06 and the “trimming threshold” and “keyness explorer” in Chapter 11 can all be used to carry out these four comparisons.

str_extract(agenda_labels, "war")
str_extract(str_to_lower(agenda_labels), "war")
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> str_extract(agenda_labels, "war")
[1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA
> str_extract(str_to_lower(agenda_labels), "war")
[1] NA    NA    "war" NA    "war" NA    "war" NA
How to read the output
  • NA means the pattern was not found in that label, not that the whole document is missing.
  • Patterns are case-sensitive by default: "war" matches none of the original labels; after str_to_lower(), labels 3, 5 and 7 all match.
  • Note that label 5 is “ROYAL NAVY (GERMAN SUBMARINE WARFARE)”—the match is part of warfare. Word boundaries in the next section deal with exactly this.

R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)

[1] "1945/jan/16" "1945/jan/16" "1945/jan/24" "1945/jan/30" "1945/jan/31"
"\\d"
One digit → the first digit of every URL is “1”.
"\\d+"
One or more digits → the first run of digits, “1945”.
str_extract_all(…, "\\d+")
All runs of digits: year, day, plus 5, 0407, 0, 19450116, 118… from the URL anchor (these are not dates!).
"\\d{4}/[a-z]{3}/\\d{2}"
Four digits / three lowercase letters / two digits → “1945/jan/16”.

example_text <- c(
  "The war changed British politics.",
  "The committee moved towards a compromise.",
  "Post-war trade was discussed."
)

str_detect(str_to_lower(example_text), "war")
str_detect(str_to_lower(example_text), "\\bwar\\b")
R console output (run locally: R 4.5.3, quanteda 4.5.1, quanteda.textstats 0.97.2, quanteda.textplots 0.96.1, stringr 1.6.0, dplyr 1.2.1, ggplot2 4.0.3; Linux aarch64)
> example_text <- c(
+   "The war changed British politics.",
+   "The committee moved towards a compromise.",
+   "Post-war trade was discussed."
+ )
> str_detect(str_to_lower(example_text), "war")
[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE
> str_detect(str_to_lower(example_text), "\\bwar\\b")
[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

The loose pattern matches all three sentences; \\bwar\\b excludes towards but still matches post-war, because the hyphen counts as a word boundary. Choose the rule that matches the meaning you want. (Lab notes)

R · clean_agenda_labels (W2/lab/answers/Lab_Session_W2_Answers.R)
hoc <- hoc |>
  mutate(
    agenda_clean = agenda |>
      str_to_lower() |>
      str_squish() |>
      str_replace_all("\\s*\\[.*\\]", ""),
    agenda_clean = case_when(
      agenda_clean == "business of the house" ~ "Business of the House",
      agenda_clean == "points of order" ~ "Points of Order",
      agenda_clean == "topical questions" ~ "Topical Questions",
      str_detect(agenda_clean, "^engagements") ~ "Engagements",
      TRUE ~ str_to_title(agenda_clean)
    )
  )

hoc |>
  count(agenda_clean, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)

str_to_lower() |> str_squish()
Unify case and collapse whitespace.
str_replace_all("\\s*\\[.*\\]", "")
Delete bracketed context (note that this uses the greedy .*, the case from Chapter 04, slide 20; agenda labels usually have only one pair of brackets, so the impact is small).
case_when(…)
Gives four common agendas a unified spelling; merges all labels beginning with engagements into “Engagements”; uses str_to_title() for the rest.
The Lab's reminder: cleaning is not neutral

Merging all labels that begin with Engagements may help a descriptive plot, but it also removes detail. Record your cleaning choices. Also note the first row of the output: 206 agendas are NA, and cleaning does not fill anything in for them.

  text2238.2 
               "Gentleman's question on Northern Ireland, I shall, of course, be repeating and emphasising my personal commitment to the guarantee to the people of Northern Ireland, which is enshrined in law in this country." 
  text2238.3

  text2238.4

"I stress that the Government have kept 413 the pension slightly ahead of the rise in the cost of living, and our first increase actually provided an additional amount to make up for the shortfall of the previous Government."
Reading the output: sentence boundaries split wrongly
  • text2238.1 is only “With regard to the right hon.”, and the next sentence starts with “Gentleman's question…”: the period in hon. is an abbreviation, not the end of a sentence. This is exactly what the Lab warns about.
  • text2238.5 contains “the Government have kept 413 the pension”: this 413 looks like a Hansard column number that slipped into the text (our observation, not from the lecture)—the “recording conventions” discussed in Chapter 03; it becomes a number token.

Self-check

1. str_extract(agenda_labels, "war") returns NA everywhere, but after str_to_lower() it matches 3. Why?
Lab: Pattern matching is case-sensitive by default.
2. corpus_reshape(engagements_corpus, to = "sentences") turns 81 documents into 364. Which statement is false?
The total amount of text is unchanged, but the definition of “a document” has changed, so comparisons and statistics change with it.Slide 6
3. After cleaning, the top entry of agenda_clean is <NA> (206 records). What does this mean?
The first row of the frequency table of the original agenda is already NA 206 (output of Exercise 7).

Lab sections 3–4: tokens, phrases, KWIC, collocations, DFM, keyness, time trends

The Lab builds two sets of tokens: one kept as-is so KWIC can show context, and another lowercased with stopwords removed for DFM counts. This is exactly the “branching” described on slide 14.

Read the words before and after each match. A single occurrence of economy does not tell you whether the speaker evaluates the economy positively or negatively. (Lab notes) For example, in text472, “a very real practice of economy in the Royal Household”, economy means “thrift”, not the national economy—polysemy is exactly the “ambiguity requires context” point of slide 30. Also look at the European_Union output: in text1971 and text2832 the preceding word is Western, i.e., a different organization, the Western European Union; text2984 has the lowercase European_union. Even after compounding phrases, use KWIC to check what they matched (our observation).

A second set of tokens for the DFM

R · tokenize_for_dfm (W2/lab/answers/Lab_Session_W2_Answers.R)
hoc_tokens_dfm <- tokens(
  hoc_corpus,
  what = "word",
  remove_punct = TRUE,
  padding = TRUE,
  remove_symbols = TRUE,
  remove_numbers = FALSE,
  remove_url = TRUE,
  remove_separators = TRUE,
  split_hyphens = FALSE
) |>
  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"), padding = TRUE)
padding = TRUE
Removed words leave empty placeholders, so words that were not adjacent are not joined together—avoiding the “creating pairs that never existed” problem from slide 32, which matters especially for finding collocations.
remove_url = TRUE, split_hyphens = FALSE
Removes URLs; hyphenated words like post-war stay one token.
tokens_tolower() |> tokens_remove(stopwords("en"), padding = TRUE)
Lowercases and removes 175 English stopwords (including not).

How to read the output
  • lambda (λ) is the strength of association and z its standardized value; the list is sorted by λ. hong kong (λ ≈ 18.02), sri lanka and per cent (724 times) come first.
  • northern ireland occurs 338 times with λ ≈ 12.41—the “statistical collocation candidate” example on slide 33.
  • sinn fein (17) and sinn fã (15) both appear: the same party name is split into two features by an encoding problem (Chapter 03).
  • High association does not mean useful: slide 33 asks you to inspect usage before adding it to a measurement rule.
R · compound_collocations_for_dfm (W2/lab/answers/Lab_Session_W2_Answers.R)
hoc_collocation_phrases <- hoc_collocations |>
  filter(lambda > 10) |>
  pull(collocation) |>
  phrase()

hoc_tokens_dfm <- tokens_compound(
  hoc_tokens_dfm,
  pattern = hoc_collocation_phrases
)

hoc_tokens_dfm <- tokens_remove(hoc_tokens_dfm, "")

Collocations with λ > 10 are glued into a single token, and tokens_remove(hoc_tokens_dfm, "") then removes the empty strings left by padding.

textplot_keyness(conservative_keyness, n = 20) (generated locally in R).
How to read the output
  • Keyness compares the word use of a “target group” (Conservative) with a “reference group” (the other 22 parties combined). A positive χ² = relatively over-represented in Conservative speeches; negative = leaning toward the reference group. This is a comparison of word use, not a sentiment score. (Lab notes)
  • hon (3,303 vs. 3,266) and friend are at the top: these two words come mainly from parliamentary forms of address such as “my hon. Friend”, and may reflect speaking roles and parliamentary conventions rather than issue positions (our interpretation).
  • Words like cyberstalking (42 vs. 0), stalking, icmp (25 vs. 0) and badger shoot to the top on the strength of just a few speeches—in a sample of 5,000, one or two long speeches can dominate keyness. Before reading them, use KWIC to see which speeches they come from.

Interactive: keyness explorer (real party DFM)

⚖️Keyness explorerReal data · hoc_dfm_party_trimmed

The data are the trimmed party DFM exported from R (23 × 5,474). Choose a target party; JS computes each feature's keyness as the χ² of a 2 × 2 contingency table (no continuity correction); for both Conservative and Labour this matches the output of R's textstat_keyness() (checked automatically below).

Over-represented in the target (χ² > 0)
Over-represented in the reference (χ² < 0)
Try it: set the “minimum target count” to 20 and look at Conservative's top 15 again.

Words that appear in only a few speeches and are 0 in the reference group (e.g., cyberstalking, icmp) are partly filtered out, leaving more “general” differences. This is a sensitivity check (Full / trimmed vocabulary on slide 59): if a conclusion rests on only a few rare words, it is not robust. Note: the minimum-count filter is an exploration option added by these notes; textstat_keyness() itself has no such argument.Slide 59

Tracking a feature over time

R · conservative_economy_by_year (W2/lab/answers/Lab_Session_W2_Answers.R)
hoc_dfm_year_conservative <- dfm(hoc_tokens_dfm)

hoc_dfm_year_conservative <- dfm_subset(
  hoc_dfm_year_conservative,
  party == "Conservative"
)

hoc_dfm_year_conservative <- dfm_group(
  hoc_dfm_year_conservative,
  groups = docvars(hoc_dfm_year_conservative, "year")
)

docvars(hoc_dfm_year_conservative, "economy") <- as.numeric(
  hoc_dfm_year_conservative[, "economy"]
)

economy_by_year <- docvars(hoc_dfm_year_conservative)

ggplot(economy_by_year, aes(x = as.integer(year), y = economy)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Frequency of 'economy'",
    title = "Conservative mentions of economy in the teaching sample"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
Raw yearly counts of economy in Conservative speeches (generated locally in R).

These are raw counts in the sample. A higher point in a given year may simply mean more speeches were sampled that year, not that economy was used more often; nor does it mean more concern or more support. (Lab notes) The interactive below lets you convert raw counts into “per 1,000 tokens”.

Self-check

1. dim(hoc_dfm_party) is 23 × 30640. What is 23?
After grouping, rows are parties, columns are features, and cells are summed counts.
2. In the keyness results, cyberstalking has a very high χ² (42 vs. 0). What is the best next step?
Keyness compares word use; it is not issue salience or sentiment. Go back to the text first.Slide 51
3. Why do the tokens for the DFM use padding = TRUE?
Lab: padding helps identify collocations; this echoes the order-of-operations issue on slide 32.Slide 32

13 · Readings and discussion

Reading guide and class discussion

The course repo's W2/papers/ has two full texts: Welbers, Van Atteveldt & Benoit (2017) and Benoit et al. (2018). The reading cards are based only on these two PDFs; page numbers are journal page numbers. For other studies mentioned in the slides, these notes have no full text and only restate the slides.

In this chapter
Welbers et al. (2017)Benoit et al. (2018)Other studies (no full text)Class discussionInteractive: judging claimsInteractive: discussion prep cardSelf-check

Welbers, K., Van Atteveldt, W., & Benoit, K. (2017). Text Analysis in R. Communication Methods and Measures 11(4): 245–265. Slides 8, 14, 64

Type of articleTeacher’s corner (a teaching introduction): gives an overview of the general steps and operations of a computational text analysis project and demonstrates how to do each step in R (p. 245 abstract). It focuses mainly on bag-of-words: using only word frequencies per text and ignoring word positions (p. 246).
StructureTable 1 divides the operations into three parts—data preparation, analysis, advanced topics—and lists the packages used plus alternatives (p. 247); Figure 1 is a diagram of the order of operations (p. 247)—these are the two reproduced on slides 8 and 14.
Five data-preparation stepsimporting text, string operations, preprocessing, document-term matrix, filtering and weighting (p. 248). It stresses that the choices made in preparing text can affect accuracy, validity and findings as much as the analysis technique itself (p. 248).
EncodingRecommends making sure all text in R is UTF-8: read UTF-8 directly, or convert from a known encoding on import; when the encoding is unknown, readtext's functions can guess it (p. 249). Compare slide 16.
Preprocessingtokenization (the period in “Dr.”; Chinese and Japanese have no whitespace word boundaries, p. 250); lowercasing and stemming (SnowballC; p. 251); stopwords (p. 251); order matters: stemming before removing stopwords turns “during” into “dure”, which no longer matches the stopword list (p. 252).
DTM, trimming and weightingA DTM has documents as rows, terms as columns and counts in cells (p. 252); quanteda's dfm uses the Matrix package as a backend (p. 252); document variables can be used to group and aggregate (e.g., tweets by user or date, p. 253); filter with document-frequency thresholds, or use tf-idf to give more common terms lower weight (p. 253).
AnalysisFollowing Boumans & Trilling (2016): counting and dictionary, supervised ML, unsupervised ML, ordered from deductive to inductive, plus text statistics (pp. 254–255).
Advanced topicsadvanced NLP (lemmatization, POS, dependency parsing; spacyr and others, pp. 258–259); keeping word positions and syntax, n-grams and skipgrams—n-grams can handle negations such as “not good”, but are computationally heavier and need more data (pp. 260–261).
Link to this weekSlide 8 specifically notes that Table 1 is a historical overview from 2017: package roles and APIs have changed since (e.g., this week uses stringr, UDPipe and Flair instead).

Source: course repo W2/papers/Welbers2017.pdf (Taylor & Francis version, 22-page PDF; page numbers are journal page numbers). doi:10.1080/19312458.2017.1387238.

Benoit, K., Watanabe, K., Wang, H., Nulty, P., Obeng, A., Müller, S., & Matsuo, A. (2018). quanteda: An R package for the quantitative analysis of textual data. Journal of Open Source Software 3(30): 774. Slides 10, 25, 50, 53

What it isAn R package providing a complete workflow: corpus management, tokenization, analysis and visualization; it includes dictionary analysis, KWIC, document and feature similarity, and finding multiword expressions by scoring collocations (p. 1).
Definition of a corpusA collection of texts that includes document-level variables for each text plus metadata for the documents and the whole collection; it can be segmented by words, paragraphs or sentences, and grouped or subset by document variables (p. 1). Compare slides 15 and 23 and the Lab's corpus_subset / corpus_reshape.
TechnologyUses the ICU library via stringi for Unicode regex and word boundaries; tokens are mapped to an integer hash table for speed and memory savings; DFMs are often more than 90% sparse (p. 2).
Models and statisticstextmodel_* implements Wordscores, Wordfish, class affinity scaling, correspondence analysis, Naive Bayes and LSA; text statistics include frequencies, keyness, lexical diversity, readability, similarity and distance (p. 2).
Design principlesConsistent naming (corpus(), tokens(), dfm() create objects; corpus_*(), tokens_*(), dfm_*() return modified objects), ease of use, performance, transparency and reproducibility, and compatibility with packages such as stm, text2vec and spacyr (p. 3).
Link to this weekAlmost everything the Lab uses follows this naming scheme: tokens_compound, dfm_group, dfm_trim, textstat_keyness, textplot_keyness. The prefix tells you what object goes in and comes out.

Source: course repo W2/papers/Benoit2018.pdf (JOSS, 4 pages, CC BY 4.0). doi:10.21105/joss.00774.

Class discussion Slide 63

Pick one of the applied papers introduced earlier, and first look at its research question and one main figure or table:

  1. What is the research question? What counts as a document?
  2. How might removing words, aggregating documents or weighting affect this measurement?
  3. Beyond “preprocessing worked”, what evidence supports the authors' interpretation?

Candidates: topic models Roberts et al. (2014), Eshima et al. (2024); text scaling Slapin & Proksch (2008), Laver et al. (2003); TF-IDF applications Blumenau (2021), Bestvater & Monroe (2023).Slide 63

Ten common pitfalls

  

    
PitfallWhy it is a problemEvidence from this week

    
Treating available texts as the populationResources, incentives, media and retrieval all introduce biasSlides 4–5 Slide 5

    
Overwriting the original textYou cannot check what cleaning changedThe Lab saves agenda_clean separately Slide 18

    
Greedy regex\[.*\] deletes all the way to the last ]“Trade ” Slide 20

    
No word boundarieswar matches warfare and towardsLab word_boundary_examples

    
A standard stopword list removes negationThe meaning of d3 is reversedworkers support policy Slide 28

    
Removing words before building bigramsCreates pairs that never existedworkers_support Slide 32

    
Keeping only NOUN / VERBThe negation “不” (ADV) disappearsSlide 42 Slide 42

    
Trimming away rare but crucial wordsmin_docfreq = 2 removes notSlide 47 Slide 47

    
Treating raw counts as attentionThe denominator (speeches, tokens) differs from year to yearYearly economy plot (Chapter 11)

    
Treating keyness as position or sentimentIt is only a comparison of word use, often dominated by parliamentary language and a few long speecheshon, friend, cyberstalking (Chapter 11)
